messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Github markdown conversion
parts:
Hi:

I would like to be able to convert the ggplot2 transition guide from
pdf to Github markdown so that it could be put up on the ggplot2 wiki
which resides on Github. Yihui's demo on the knitr website answered
some of the basic questions I had, but I still have several left. This
is a 41-page .Rnw -> knitr -> pdf document broken up into seven
sections + references, so I'm considering breaking this up into
separate .md files and then creating a header page to point to the
individual sections, but I'm certainly willing to entertain
alternative ways to go. Right now, it uses a TOC generated by LaTeX
with hyperref.

I've been watching the recent thread on this list involving conversion
to several different types of rendering modes but haven't had the time
until now to give it sufficient attention. My questions revolve around
the following subjects:

* This document has several tables, but they are concentrated in one
section - how does one use knitr to produce tables in markdown? I
noticed that either Carl Boettiger or Andrew Redd had posted a
function to create such tables and am rather interested in how it
works.
* In several places, multiple graphs are aligned horizontally in a
single row - how can I maintain that in the markdown version?
* How to maintain the global settings in \SweaveOpts and in the
setup code chunk and how to reset them locally via individual code
chunks?
* I don't need this particular feature for the ggplot2 doc, but I
would be interested in learning more details about how to convert from
a given knitr rendering mode (e.g. pdf, markdown) to Word for
consulting purposes. (I want to stay away from Word as much as
possible but corporate clients often get upset if they don't get
reports in Word format. A reasonable compromise is for me to get what
I want and the client to get what he/she wants :)


I'm happy to provide a test document and a summary/tutorial of how to
convert among different rendering modes but need a little guidance to
get going. I'll go back over the recent mails and glean what I can,
but if someone has a ready example with some of the features mentioned
above to help me see the light sooner, that would be great. The
development of this package over the past three or four months has
been astounding - it's a challenge keeping up with the pace of new and
improved features, but it certainly is exhilarating to participate in
a new paradigm for literate programming.

As always, thanks in advance for any help.


Best regards,
Dennis

You can still use \SweaveOpts{} if you run pat_rnw() before you knit()
the markdown file. Or you can use the default syntax for markdown,
e.g. <!--roptions dev='png', fig.width=5, fig.height=5 --> see this
example:

https://raw.github.com/yihui/knitr/master/inst/examples/knitr-upload_knit_.md
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/inst/examples/knitr-upload.md

and technical details at http://yihui.name/knitr/patterns

>  * I don't need this particular feature for the ggplot2 doc, but I
> would be interested in learning more details about how to convert from
> a given knitr rendering mode (e.g. pdf, markdown) to Word for
> consulting purposes. (I want to stay away from Word as much as
> possible but corporate clients often get upset if they don't get
> reports in Word format. A reasonable compromise is for me to get what
> I want and the client to get what he/she wants :)

It is easy to convert markdown files to (Open or Microsoft) Office
formats with pandoc. You can knit the attached markdown file and run
pandoc in the command window:

pandoc knitr-minimal.md -o knitr-minimal.docx

then you get a reasonably good MS Office 2007 document, which should
make your clients happy.
